To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the CP violation in the standard model is too small to explain the CP asymmetry a J / ψ K S and that supersymmetry is needed.

the smallness of the CP violating phases is a natural outcome of the supersymmetric models with universal Yukawa couplings, and that this feature is crucial for a successful description of the CP violation in B physics.

the small CP violation in the standard model and the large value of a J / ψK S are both naturally accommodated in a supersymmetric extension with universal strength of quark Yukawa couplings, but that a large amount of supersymmetric CP violation is needed to explain the data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new class of models which have a very small amount of CP violating phases in the quark mass matrix, and a significant amount of supersymmetric CP violation.
the CP problem and the implications of the new data on CP violation for supersymmetry.

the following questions: What is the source of CP violation in the standard model, what are the implications of the smallness of the CP violation in the quark sector, what are the experimental consequences of supersymmetry, and what are the implications for the search for new physics?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CP problem in supersymmetric models is not a serious problem, provided that the CP violating phase is not too large.
the supersymmetric model with universal couplings and small CP violating phases provides an attractive framework for the standard model.
a supersymmetric extension with universal strength of the Yukawa couplings is consistent with the present data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CP problem is solved in this class of supersymmetric models with small CP violating phases.
a supersymmetric extension to the standard model with small CP violating phases is possible and the experimental results are consistent with this picture.

the supersymmetric contribution to the electric dipole moment is large enough to satisfy all the experimental constraints and the supersymmetric contribution is also large enough to explain the CP asymmetry observed in the B system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CP problem can be solved in the framework of a supersymmetric theory with a rationale for the observed smallness of the CP violating phases in nature.

the smallness of the CP phases in the Yukawa couplings is an important constraint on the supersymmetric parameter space and the supersymmetric CP phases are the most important source of CP violation in the supersymmetric model.
a supersymmetric extension to the standard model with small CP violating phases is a viable framework for explaining the CP violation in B -mesons and the neutron electric dipole moment.
